nameStory: Thymeleaf sandmat gets its name from its tiny leaves that resemble those of thyme, the aromatic herb you might grow in your garden. The "sandmat" part describes how this little spurge spreads in a flat mat across sandy or disturbed ground, creating a carpet-like appearance.
description: Thymeleaf sandmat is a small, low-growing annual plant that hugs the ground in a spreading mat formation. This tiny member of the spurge family rarely grows taller than a few inches, but can spread outward up to a foot across. Like all spurges, it produces a milky white sap when broken and has very small, inconspicuous flowers. You'll need to look closely to appreciate this diminutive plant that's easily overlooked underfoot.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a flat, spreading mat that hugs the ground, with stems radiating outward from the center like spokes of a wheel

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Tiny oval leaves, usually less than 1/4 inch long, that feel smooth and slightly succulent between your fingers, arranged oppositely on the stems

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Extremely small whitish or pinkish flowers clustered in leaf joints, so tiny you might mistake them for seeds at first glance

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Thin, reddish or green stems that break easily and immediately ooze white milky sap that feels sticky on your fingers

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Tiny three-chambered capsules that split open with an audible pop when ripe, shooting seeds several feet away

habitat: Look for thymeleaf sandmat in sandy, disturbed soils like roadsides, parking lot edges, gardens, and waste areas throughout New England. It particularly thrives in compacted or poor soils where other plants struggle to establish. This adaptable little plant often appears in sidewalk cracks, gravel driveways, and sandy beaches.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate in late spring when soil warms, with tiny seedlings first appearing as small rosettes of oval leaves.
seasonality.summer: Plants reach full size and flower throughout summer, forming their characteristic spreading mats with continuous tiny blooms.
seasonality.fall: Seed capsules ripen and explosively disperse in late summer and early fall, with plants beginning to turn reddish before dying.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants die completely, leaving only seeds in the soil to sprout the following year.

funFact: When thymeleaf sandmat's seed capsules ripen, they explode with enough force to launch seeds up to 15 feet away - you can actually hear the tiny pops if you listen carefully on a quiet day!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other small sandmat spurges, especially prostrate sandmat and matted sandmat. Thymeleaf sandmat's leaves are more oval and succulent-feeling compared to the narrower, more linear leaves of its relatives. The spreading, symmetrical mat growth pattern helps distinguish it from the more sprawling, irregular growth of similar species.
contextualKnowledge: Like all spurges, thymeleaf sandmat contains a milky latex sap that can cause skin irritation in sensitive individuals. Despite being in the same family as the holiday poinsettia, this humble ground-hugger couldn't look more different from its showy tropical relative.
compareHints: Among New England's spurges, thymeleaf sandmat is distinguished by its ground-hugging mat formation and tiny thyme-like leaves. Spotted spurge has similar prostrate growth but larger leaves with dark spots, while cypress spurge grows upright with needle-like leaves. Seaside sandmat grows in similar mats but has even smaller, more linear leaves and is restricted to coastal areas.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike other spurges in New England that typically have broader, more conventional leaves, cypress spurge is instantly recognizable by its needle-like foliage.
Among New England's spurges, spotted spurge is unique for its ground-hugging mat formation and distinctly spotted leaves.
Among New England's spurges, seaside sandmat is unique in its completely prostrate, mat-forming habit and coastal habitat.
Among New England spurges, slender leafy spurge is distinguished by its tall, narrow growth form and lance-shaped leaves.
Among New England's spurges, nodding spurge is distinguished by its prostrate, mat-forming growth and drooping flower clusters.
Unlike other New England spurges which are mostly weedy annuals with thin leaves, Donkey Tail is a perennial succulent with thick, fleshy foliage.
Among New England's sandmat spurges, Wormseed Sandmat is distinguished by its perfectly circular growth pattern and distinctively ridged seeds.
Among New England spurges, caper spurge is unique for its large size and architectural growth habit - most other spurges are low-growing weeds or small garden plants.
Unlike the tall, weedy leafy spurge or the ground-hugging spotted spurge, cushion spurge maintains a perfectly rounded, compact form.
Among New England spurges, petty spurge is one of the smallest and most delicate-looking species.
Flowering spurge towers over most of its spurge relatives in New England, which tend to be low, mat-forming plants like spotted spurge or cypress spurge.
Snow-on-the-mountain is easily distinguished from other New England spurges by its distinctive white-margined leaves - most other spurges in our region have plain green foliage.

Leafy spurge stands out from other New England spurges by its tall, upright growth and dense leafy appearance - most of its relatives like spotted spurge and prostrate sandmat are low, sprawling plants.
Among New England spurges, graceful spurge stands out for its relatively tall, upright growth compared to the ground-hugging spotted spurge or prostrate sandmat.
Sweet spurge stands out from other New England spurges by its clumping perennial growth habit and relatively large, oval leaves.
Among New England spurges, green poinsettia stands out for its distinctly hairy, toothed leaves - most other spurges have smooth or nearly smooth leaves.
Unlike the needle-like leaves of cypress spurge or the spotted stems of spotted spurge, David's spurge has broader, toothed leaves arranged in opposite pairs.
Unlike other New England spurges that have broader, more typical-looking leaves, grassleaf spurge's ultra-narrow foliage makes it unique in the region.
Among New England's spurges, prostrate sandmat is uniquely flat-growing - most other spurges like cypress spurge or flowering spurge grow upright.
Unlike cypress spurge with its needle-like leaves or spotted spurge that grows as a low mat, eggleaf spurge stands upright with distinctly oval, toothed leaves.
Compared to other New England spurges, Florida hammock sandmat is distinguished by its exceptionally small size and extremely low, tight mat-forming habit.
Matted sandmat is flatter and more perfectly mat-forming than most other spurges in our region.
Among New England's spurges, ribseed sandmat is distinguished by its extremely rare occurrence and the ribbed seeds that give it its name.
